headlines.article_text: Anthropic IPO live updates: ANT stock price and Nasdaq debut Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu watch now VIDEO 5:16 05:16 Anthropic raises $81B+ in historic IPO: Here's what to know Squawk Box Anthropic is set for its long-awaited Nasdaq debut on Thursday, after the artificial intelligence lab raised over $81 billion in a record IPO , surpassing SpaceX 's offering in June. The Claude creator sold 980 million shares at $83 a piece on Wednesday, lifting the size and price of its offering. Its fully diluted market cap sits at around $1.5 trillion. The 5-year-old company captivated the corporate world with its Claude AI models and products, which have fueled its meteoric rise this year. Anthropic said in its prospectus that it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up a staggering 1,200% from the same period last year. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic has faced sharp criticism over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, including by President Donald Trump and other senior government officials. Highlights so far: Protesters gather outside the Nasdaq Indicated to open at $105 per share Daniela Amodei gives a shoutout to mom Dario Amodei addresses debt and landing an investment-grade credit rating Spotted: Executives sporting "Clawd" pins at Nasdaq Dario Amodei renews pledge to pace frontier AI development Retail demand for ANT was the largest in history Anthropic employees set to get rich CNBC's reporters are covering Anthropic's IPO live on air and online from our bureaus in San Francisco and Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, and from the Nasdaq in New York City. Samyukta Lakshmi | Bloomberg | Getty Images Amodei told JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon in a fireside chat on Friday that he thinks talent and culture are the "most important things" that drive a company's success, which is why he and his co-founders have tried to place so much emphasis on those areas at Anthropic. Anthropic requires every employee to pass a culture interview, which is taken very seriously, Amodei said. He added that he spends roughly half of his time focusing on talent and culture at the company. "We've been very disciplined about turning down people who are deeply technically talented, but who don't fit our culture," Amodei said. "We don't want people who are jerks. We don't want people who try to steal the show and don't work well with others. We don't want people who aren't oriented towards the public benefit." Amodei also regularly holds DVQs, which stands for "Dario Vision Quests," where he speaks in front of the entire company. He said he tries to update employees by talking honestly and avoiding "corpo speak." "It means that the leaders of the company can trust the employees," Amodei said. "The employees of the company can trust the leaders of the company to be candid. Everyone feels that we're being honest with them, and that has this enormous value." — Ashley Capoot 11 Min Ago Ben Reitzes: 'The leverage here could be insane' watch now VIDEO 4:23 04:23 Melius initiates coverage of Anthropic with buy rating and price target of $155 Squawk on the Street Ben Reitzes, Head of Technology Research at Melius, said growth and leverage as well as efficiency gains outweigh margin concerns when it comes to estimating Anthropic's future growth path. "They're ahead of the game in models, making them more efficient, and their cost to train is going down, and the speed to train is going down. So they're going to be putting out models at such a rapid clip that are on the frontier," Reitzes told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "That makes them more valuable and worth paying for." Santiago | Getty Images Anthropic prioritized allocating shares to institutional investors it had relationships with, according to people familiar with the details, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That meant roughly half of the firms that placed orders were left empty handed, they said. It's normal in most IPOs for some portion of institutional investors not to receive any allocation, but that happened to be a higher number than usual for this offering, one person said. Anthropic's management team had experience working with institutional investors from raising capital through private rounds, so the company had a strong view of what would make up a good shareholder base construction, the person said. Retail allocation came in at around 15%, the people said. Anthropic had estimated that about 20% of the offering would go to retail, as CNBC previously reported, a higher percentage than the typical 5% to 10% allotment. — Leslie Picker and Ashley Capoot 20 Min Ago Protestors gather outside the Nasdaq Demonstrators hold a banner during the Anthropic PBC initial public offering (IPO) at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. Adam Gray | Bloomberg | Getty Images Protestors are gathering outside of the Nasdaq ahead of the listing. The New York City Democratic Socialists of America shared a post on Instagram on Wednesday encouraging demonstrators to attend a rally at 9 a.m. ET. on Thursday. The group said Anthropic "is driving the AI bubble to get rich quick before the bubble bursts." "Join our rally to send a message to all Big Tech oligarchs and demand a freeze to reckless AI development and destruction," the group said. Other organizations, including Climate Defiance, Act Up and New York Communities for Change are also sponsoring the protest. — Ashley Capoot 22 Min Ago Goldman and Morgan Stanley led the IPO As with SpaceX's offering, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led Anthropic's IPO. Anthropic made shares available to retail investors through brokerages including Charles Schwab, Fidelity, Robinhood, SoFi, E-Trade and some of their respective affiliates, the AI startup said in an IPO prospectus. Many of them have "anti-flipping" policies meant to discourage investors who purchase IPO shares from dumping them fast. These policies apply only to retail investors who place an order with their brokerage firm to buy the Anthropic IPO at its offering price — something many investors don't have access to. For example, Fidelity clients who sell IPO shares within the first 15 calendar days from the start of trading in the secondary market would be barred from participating in future stock IPOs through the brokerage. headlines.article_text: amazon-nyc-delivery-protection-act Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Amazon is showing pop-up notices to some users of its app and website warning against a New York City bill that aims to disrupt its contracted delivery model. A banner on its homepage states the bill, dubbed the Delivery Protection Act, "could add up to $5 per order." Amazon has lobbied heavily against the proposed legislation, while New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani backed the bill earlier this year. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT An Amazon driver loads packages into a delivery van at an Amazon delivery station in Alpharetta, Georgia, Nov. 28, 2022. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images Amazon is taking its fight against a New York City delivery bill, which has been backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani , to its shopping website and app. Some users who open the company's shopping app or website report being served with pop-ups and banners warning that the New York City Council "could add up to $5 per order" if it passes Intro 518, or the Delivery Protection Act. The bill would require Amazon to employ its army of third-party delivery companies directly, disrupting the contractor model it has relied on since 2018. Amazon uses a network of thousands of small companies, who often solely work for Amazon, to handle the last-mile portion of shipments, in an effort to speed up deliveries and control more of its logistics operations. "If this legislation passes, we'd no longer be able to work with them, and we'd be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city," Amazon's in-app message states. "That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees." The proposed legislation was introduced in February and is awaiting review by City Council Speaker Julie Menin. Amazon also posted a statement on its company website where it often publishes its policy positions . But rarely has it used its valuable e-commerce site and app real estate to push its perspectives. Other tech companies including Uber and Lyft have similarly used their apps to advocate for or against legislation in the past. Amazon's pop-up notices and a stationary banner on its store homepage direct users to a form where they can "contact your council member to oppose Intro 518." The Delivery Protection Act has received a swell of support from labor groups, including the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which has sought to unionize Amazon delivery and warehouse workers. Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon's subcontractor model "leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets." He's argued the bill would lead to safer working conditions for drivers, and allow the city to "regulate last-mile operations." Amazon has lobbied heavily against the bill, while business groups have launched local advertising campaigns, and warned they may sue the city if the bill passes.
